nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority, and let $t$ be a tree. Then $p$ holds at every node of $t$ if and only if $p(k, v, n)$ holds for every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ such that the entry $(k, v, n)$ occurs as a node of $t$.
nodes.title: Treap all-nodes predicate via node membership

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on keys and let $t$ be a tree. Then the key of every node of $t$ satisfies $p$ if and only if $p(k)$ holds for every key $k$ that occurs in $t$.
nodes.title: Treap all-nodes predicate on keys via key membership

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority. A tree satisfies $p$ at every node when $p(k, v, n)$ holds for the key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ of each of its nodes. By recursion, this holds for the empty tree, and holds for a node exactly when it holds for the left subtree, $p$ holds at the node's key, value and priority, and it holds for the right subtree.
nodes.title: Treap predicate holding at every node

nodes.summary: For a tree $t$ and a list $s$ of key-value pairs, the traversal of $t$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion: for the empty tree it is $s$, and for a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$ and right subtree $r$ it is the traversal of $l$ onto the list obtained by putting $(k, v)$ in front of the traversal of $r$ onto $s$. The result is the key-value pairs of $t$ in inorder, priorities dropped, followed by $s$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder traversal onto a suffix

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a key, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ is the inorder list of $L$ followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents after erasure

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree, $k$ a key, $v$ a value and $n$ a natural-number priority, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $n$ into $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents after insertion

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is the inorder list of $l$ followed by the inorder list of $r$.
nodes.title: Treap merge concatenates inorder contents

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a natural-number priority $n$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $n$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder list of $l$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $r$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents of a node

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a pivot key, and let splitting $t$ at $k$ produce a lower tree $L$, an optional value-priority pair found at $k$, and an upper tree $G$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$ if the split found a pair with value $v$ (and by nothing if it found none), followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents split at a pivot

nodes.summary: The contents of a tree $t$ is the list of its key-value pairs in inorder (left subtree, then node, then right subtree), with priorities dropped. It is defined as the inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list, which takes linear time.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $t$, deleting $k$ from $t$ splits $t$ at $k$ and returns the priority-guided merge of the part of the split below $k$ with the part above $k$; the entry the split finds at $k$, if any, is dropped.
nodes.title: Treap deletion

nodes.summary: If two trees $l$ and $r$ are both heap-ordered in their priorities, then the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Merging preserves heap order

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be a heap-ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Treap split preserves heap order

nodes.summary: A tree is heap-ordered when the priority of every node is at most the priority of every node below it. Recursively, the empty tree is heap-ordered, and a node with priority $p$ is heap-ordered when its left and right subtrees are heap-ordered and every node in them has priority at least $p$.
nodes.title: Heap order of treap priorities

nodes.summary: If a nonempty tree whose root has priority $p$ is heap-ordered, then every node of the tree, the root included, has priority at least $p$.
nodes.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree has minimal priority

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type, a value $v$, a priority $p$ and a tree $t$, inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ splits $t$ at $k$, drops the entry the split finds at $k$ if any, merges the part below $k$ with the single node $(k, v, p)$, and then merges the result with the part above $k$; all merges are priority-guided.
nodes.title: Treap insertion

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ and a tree $t$, some pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys occurring in the inorder contents

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a priority $p$, the inorder key list of the node with left subtree $l$, entry $(k, v, p)$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder key list of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder key list of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder keys of a node

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, if a tree is ordered as a binary search tree (at every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger than the node's key), then its inorder key list has no duplicates.
nodes.title: Treap keys are distinct

nodes.summary: The inorder key list of a tree $t$ is the list of first components of the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$, that is, the keys of $t$ in inorder.
nodes.title: Inorder key list of a treap

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup agrees with the inorder contents

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.
nodes.title: Treap lookup finds exactly the stored entries

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ returns no value.
nodes.title: Erased keys are not found

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup after insertion

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the number of nodes visited by the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ is at most the number of nodes of $t$.
nodes.title: Lookup cost is at most the tree size

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the value component of the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ (ignoring the visit count) equals the result of looking up $k$ in $t$.
nodes.title: Costed lookup returns the ordinary lookup result

nodes.summary: The costed lookup of a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type returns a possibly absent value together with a natural number counting the visited nodes. On the empty tree it returns no value and cost $0$. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, if $k < r$ it returns the result of the costed lookup of $k$ in the left subtree with cost increased by $1$; if $r < k$ it does the same with the right…
nodes.title: Lookup with cost

nodes.summary: Looking up a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type follows the binary search tree comparisons. The empty tree gives no value. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, the lookup continues in the left subtree if $k < r$, continues in the right subtree if $r < k$, and otherwise returns $v$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$, key $k$ and value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.
nodes.title: Inorder contents list the treap's entries

nodes.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, $k$ is the key of some node of the merge of $l$ and $r$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $l$ or of some node of $r$.
nodes.title: Keys of a merged treap

nodes.summary: If a key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree $t$, that is, some node of $t$ stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$, then $k$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Entry membership implies key membership in a treap

nodes.summary: A key $k$ is a key of a treap tree when it is stored at some node: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $k$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $k$ belongs to $L$, or $k = r$, or $k$ belongs to $R$.
nodes.title: Key membership in a treap tree

nodes.summary: For every treap tree $t$ and key $k$, $k$ occurs in the inorder key list of $t$ if and only if $k$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: The inorder key list lists exactly the keys of a treap

nodes.summary: A key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree when some node stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$: the empty tree has no entries, and $(k, v, p)$ is an entry of a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$, root value $w$, root priority $q$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when it is an entry of $L$, or $k = r$, $v = w$ and $p = q$, or it is an entry of $R$.
nodes.title: Entry membership in a treap tree

nodes.summary: The merge of two treap trees is defined recursively. Merging the empty tree with a tree $T$, or $T$ with the empty tree, gives $T$. If both trees are nodes, with root priorities $p$ for the first and $q$ for the second, then when $p \le q$ the result keeps the root of the first tree and its left subtree, and its right subtree is the merge of the first tree's right subtree with the second tree; otherwise the result…
nodes.title: Treap merge

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If a treap tree $t$ is ordered, then its inorder key list is strictly increasing: each key in the list is smaller than every key after it.
nodes.title: Inorder keys of an ordered treap are strictly increasing

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If treap trees $L$ and $R$ are both ordered and every key of $L$ is smaller than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Treap merge preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both ordered.
nodes.title: Treap split preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: For a key type equipped with a relation $<$, a treap tree is ordered when it is empty, or when it is a node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are both ordered, every key $x$ in the left subtree satisfies $x < k$, and every key $y$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < y$.
nodes.title: Ordered treap tree

nodes.summary: The root priority of a treap tree is an optional natural number: it is absent for the empty tree, and for a node it is the priority stored at that node.
nodes.title: Root priority of a treap tree

nodes.summary: For keys equipped with a binary relation $<$, two trees $L$ and $R$ are separated when $a < b$ for every key $a$ occurring at a node of $L$ and every key $b$ occurring at a node of $R$.
nodes.title: Separated treap trees

nodes.summary: The size of a tree is its number of nodes, computed recursively: the empty tree has size $0$, and a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ has size equal to the size of $L$ plus one plus the size of $R$.
nodes.title: Size of a treap tree

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order and let $T$ be an ordered tree. For every pivot $p$, every key of the lower tree obtained by splitting $T$ at $p$ is strictly less than $p$, and every key of the upper tree is strictly greater than $p$.
nodes.title: Split bounds for an ordered treap

nodes.summary:
For key type $\kappa$ and value type $
u$, a split result consists of a lower tree, an optional entry given by a value in $
u$ together with a natural-number priority, and an upper tree, where both trees are treap trees with keys in $\kappa$ and values in $
u$.
nodes.title: Result of a treap split

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order, and write $(L, k, v, q, R)$ for the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $q$ and right subtree $R$. Splitting a tree at a pivot $p$ returns a split result, defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree splits into two empty trees and no entry. For a node $(L, k, v, q, R)$: if $k < p$, split $R$ at $p$ into a lower tree $R_1$, an optional entry $e$ and an…
nodes.title: Treap split

nodes.summary: For a type $\kappa$ of keys and a type $\nu$ of values, a treap tree is either empty or a node made of a left subtree, a key in $\kappa$, a value in $\nu$, a natural-number priority and a right subtree. Trees are finite, and no ordering of keys or priorities is imposed; the treap invariants are stated separately.
nodes.title: Treap trees

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$ the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from it is again a valid treap.
nodes.title: Erasing from a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$, value $v$ and natural-number priority $q$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $q$ is again a valid treap.
nodes.title: Inserting into a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If $L$ and $R$ are valid treaps and every key of $L$ is strictly less than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is a valid treap.
nodes.title: Merging separated treaps preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, then for every pivot $p$, both the lower tree and the upper tree obtained by splitting it at $p$ are valid treaps.
nodes.title: Splitting a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: A binary tree whose nodes each carry a key, a value and a natural-number priority, with keys compared by a relation $<$ (any `LT` instance; no order axioms are assumed), is a valid treap when it satisfies both of the following at every node: every key in the left subtree is less than the node's key and the node's key is less than every key in the right subtree (search-tree order with respect to $<$), and the node's…
nodes.title: Valid treap

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
